**Modulus.**  
Write  

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}= (p+q)^{2}+5pq .
\]

If this is a square, say \(m^{2}\), then  

\[
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq .
\]

Thus the two factors on the left are positive divisors of \(5pq\) whose product is \(5pq\).

**Witness / case split.**  
Since \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of \(5pq\) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Hence we must have  

\[
\{\,m-p-q,\;m+p+q\,\}=\{d,\;5pq/d\}
\]

for some \(d\) in the above list.  Because \(m-p-q<m+p+q\), we set  

\[
m-p-q=d,\qquad m+p+q=\frac{5pq}{d}.
\]

Adding the two equations gives  

\[
2m = d+\frac{5pq}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
m = \frac{d}{2}+\frac{5pq}{2d}.
\]

Since \(m\) is an integer, \(d\) must divide \(5pq\) and also make the right‑hand side integral; this forces \(d\) to be even or to make \(5pq/d\) even.  Checking the eight possibilities for \(d\) yields only two admissible cases:

* \(d= p\) gives \(m-p-q=p\) and \(m+p+q=5q\).  Solving gives \(p=3,\;q=11\).
* \(d= q\) gives the symmetric solution \(p=11,\;q=3\).

All other choices lead to contradictions (either \(m-p-q\le0\) or non‑integral \(m\)).

**Identity / bound.**  
The remaining possibility is \(d=5\).  Then  

\[
m-p-q=5,\qquad m+p+q=pq,
\]

which forces \(p=q=5\); but \(5\) is not a solution of the original equation (plugging in gives \(5^{2}+7\cdot5^{2}+5^{2}=9\cdot5^{2}\) which is not a square).  Hence this case is discarded.

**Conclusion.**  
The only solutions are  

\[
(p,q)=(3,11)\quad\text{or}\quad(p,q)=(11,3),
\]

and the trivial case \(p=q\) (which gives \((p+q)^{2}+5p^{2}\) never a square for a prime \(p\)).  Therefore  

\[
\exists m,\;p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]

holds exactly for the two ordered pairs above, with the witnesses  

\[
m=13\;\text{when}\;(p,q)=(3,11),\qquad 
m=13\;\text{when}\;(p,q)=(11,3).
\]

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Modulus.**  
Write  

\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}= (p+q)^{2}+5pq .
\]

If this is a square, say \(m^{2}\), then  

\[
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq .
\]

Thus the two factors on the left are positive divisors of \(5pq\) whose product is \(5pq\).

**Witness / case split.**  
Since \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of \(5pq\) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Hence we must have  

\[
\{\,m-p-q,\;m+p+q\,\}=\{d,\;5pq/d\}
\]

for some \(d\) in the above list.  Because \(m-p-q<m+p+q\), we set  

\[
m-p-q=d,\qquad m+p+q=\frac{5pq}{d}.
\]

Adding the two equations gives  

\[
2m = d+\frac{5pq}{d}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
m = \frac{d}{2}+\frac{5pq}{2d}.
\]

Since \(m\) is an integer, \(d\) must divide \(5pq\) and also make the right‑hand side integral; this forces \(d\) to be even or to make \(5pq/d\) even.  Checking the eight possibilities for \(d\) yields only two admissible cases:

* \(d= p\) gives \(m-p-q=p\) and \(m+p+q=5q\).  Solving gives \(p=3,\;q=11\).
* \(d= q\) gives the symmetric solution \(p=11,\;q=3\).

All other choices lead to contradictions (either \(m-p-q\le0\) or non‑integral \(m\)).

**Identity / bound.**  
The remaining possibility is \(d=5\).  Then  

\[
m-p-q=5,\qquad m+p+q=pq,
\]

which forces \(p=q=5\); but \(5\) is not a solution of the original equation (plugging in gives \(5^{2}+7\cdot5^{2}+5^{2}=9\cdot5^{2}\) which is not a square).  Hence this case is discarded.

**Conclusion.**  
The only solutions are  

\[
(p,q)=(3,11)\quad\text{or}\quad(p,q)=(11,3),
\]

and the trivial case \(p=q\) (which gives \((p+q)^{2}+5p^{2}\) never a square for a prime \(p\)).  Therefore  

\[
\exists m,\;p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]

holds exactly for the two ordered pairs above, with the witnesses  

\[
m=13\;\text{when}\;(p,q)=(3,11),\qquad 
m=13\;\text{when}\;(p,q)=(11,3).
\]

open Nat

theorem rmo_2001_2 (p q : ℕ) (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hq : Nat.Prime q) :
  (∃ m : ℕ, p^2 + 7*p*q + q^2 = m^2) ↔
    (p = q ∨ (p = 3 ∧ q = 11) ∨ (p = 11 ∧ q = 3)) := by
  constructor
  intro h
  rcases h with ⟨m, hm⟩
  have h1 : m > p + q := by
    nlinarith [Nat.Prime.two_le hp, Nat.Prime.two_le hq]
  have h2 : m < p + q + 5 * p * q := by
    nlinarith [Nat.Prime.two_le hp, Nat.Prime.two_le hq]

      have h4 : m ≥ p + q := by omega

        have h7 : (p + q) ^ 2 = p ^ 2 + 2 * p * q + q ^ 2 := by ring
        rw [h6, h7]

      have h8 : m - p - q ≥ 0 := by omega
      have h9 : m + p + q > 0 := by nlinarith [Nat.Prime.pos hp, Nat.Prime.pos hq]

      rw [h10] at *
      exact h5

    have h4 : m - p - q ∣ 5 * p * q := by
      use m + p + q
      exact h3.symm ▸ by ring
    skip
  case mpr =>
    sorry

**Key fact – factorisation**  
From  
\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]
complete the square:
\[
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – set the small factor**  
Put  
\[
d:=m-p-q\;(>0),\qquad D:=m+p+q .
\]
Then (1) gives \(dD=5pq\) and \(D-d=2(p+q)\).

**Bound – size of the small factor**  
Since \(D>d\) we have \(d\le\sqrt{5pq}\).  
Because \(p,q\) are primes, every divisor of \(5pq\) is one of  

\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]

Thus \(d\) must belong to this list.

**Case split – examine each possible \(d\)**  

| \(d\) | Equation \(dD=5pq\) gives \(D=\frac{5pq}{d}\) | Use \(D-d=2(p+q)\) to solve for \((p,q)\) |
|------|---------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| \(1\) | \(D=5pq\) → \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\) ⇒ impossible for primes |
| \(5\) | \(D=pq\) → \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) ⇒ \((p-5)(q-5)=30\). The only prime solutions are \((p,q)=(3,11)\) or \((11,3)\). |
| \(p\) | \(D=5q\) → \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) ⇒ \(3p=3q\) ⇒ \(p=q\). |
| \(q\) | symmetric to the previous case, again gives \(p=q\). |
| \(5p\) | \(D=q\) gives \(q-5p=2(p+q)\) ⇒ negative, impossible. |
| \(5q\) | symmetric, impossible. |
| \(pq\) | \(D=5\) gives \(5-pq=2(p+q)\) ⇒ negative, impossible. |
| \(5pq\) | \(D=1\) impossible because \(D>d\). |

**Induction / conclusion** – no further possibilities.  

Hence the only solutions are  

* \(p=q\) (any prime, giving \(m=p+q\)), and  
* \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\) (giving \(m=19\)).  

Thus  

\[
p = q\;\;\text{or}\;\;(p,q)=(3,11)\;\;\text{or}\;\;(p,q)=(11,3).
\]

**Key Fact:** The factorization $(m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq$ derived from completing the square.

1.  **Identity:** Rewrite $p^2+7pq+q^2=m^2$ as $(m-(p+q))(m+(p+q))=5pq$.
2.  **Bound:** Let $d = m-(p+q)$ and $D = m+(p+q)$. Then $d \cdot D = 5pq$ with $0 < d < D$.
3.  **Case Split:** Since $d$ divides $5pq$, test divisors $1, 5, p, q, 5p, 5q, pq, 5pq$.
4.  **Witness:** For each valid pair $(d, D)$, solve for $p, q$ using $D-d = 2(p+q)$.
    *   If $d=1, D=5pq$, then $2(p+q) = 5pq-1$. No solution for primes.
    *   If $d=p, D=5q$ (assuming $p<q$), then $2(p+q) = 5q-p \implies 3p=3q \implies p=q$.
    *   If $d=5, D=pq$, then $2(p+q) = pq-5$. Solutions: $(3, 11)$ and $(11, 3)$.
5.  **Conclusion:** The only solutions are $p=q$ or $\{p,q\} = \{3, 11\}$.

From  
\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]
complete the square:
\[
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the small factor**  
Set  
\[
d:=m-p-q>0,\qquad D:=m+p+q .
\]
Then (1) gives \(dD=5pq\) and \(D-d=2(p+q)\).

**Bound**  
From the hypotheses \(m>p+q\) and \(m<p+q+5pq\) we obtain  
\(1\le d\le 5pq\) and \(d<D\).  Hence \(d\) is a positive divisor of \(5pq\) that is at most \(\sqrt{5pq}\).

**Case split – possible values of \(d\)**  
The divisors of \(5pq\) not exceeding \(\sqrt{5pq}\) are  
\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]
(The hypothesis \(d<D\) eliminates the last three.)  
Thus
\[
d\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q\}.
\]

**Induction – test each case**  

* \(d=1\): then \(D=5pq\).  From \(D-d=2(p+q)\) we get \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), impossible for primes.

* \(d=5\): then \(D=pq\).  Equation \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) gives \((p-5)(q-5)=35\).  The only prime solution is \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\).

* \(d=p\): then \(D=5q\).  From \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) we obtain \(5q=3p+2q\), i.e. \(3p=3q\), so \(p=q\).

* \(d=5p\): then \(D=q\).  Since \(D<d\) this contradicts \(d<D\).

* \(d=5q\): similarly impossible.

Thus the only possibilities are  

* \(p=q\) (any prime), or  
* \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\).

A mathematician was asked how to prove this goal and answered:
**Key fact – factorisation**  
From  
\[
p^{2}+7pq+q^{2}=m^{2}
\]
complete the square:
\[
m^{2}-(p+q)^{2}=5pq\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (m-p-q)(m+p+q)=5pq .\tag{1}
\]

**Witness – the small factor**  
Set  
\[
d:=m-p-q>0,\qquad D:=m+p+q .
\]
Then (1) gives \(dD=5pq\) and \(D-d=2(p+q)\).

**Bound**  
From the hypotheses \(m>p+q\) and \(m<p+q+5pq\) we obtain  
\(1\le d\le 5pq\) and \(d<D\).  Hence \(d\) is a positive divisor of \(5pq\) that is at most \(\sqrt{5pq}\).

**Case split – possible values of \(d\)**  
The divisors of \(5pq\) not exceeding \(\sqrt{5pq}\) are  
\[
1,\;5,\;p,\;q,\;5p,\;5q,\;pq,\;5pq .
\]
(The hypothesis \(d<D\) eliminates the last three.)  
Thus
\[
d\in\{1,5,p,q,5p,5q\}.
\]

**Induction – test each case**  

* \(d=1\): then \(D=5pq\).  From \(D-d=2(p+q)\) we get \(5pq-1=2(p+q)\), impossible for primes.

* \(d=5\): then \(D=pq\).  Equation \(pq-5=2(p+q)\) gives \((p-5)(q-5)=35\).  The only prime solution is \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\).

* \(d=p\): then \(D=5q\).  From \(5q-p=2(p+q)\) we obtain \(5q=3p+2q\), i.e. \(3p=3q\), so \(p=q\).

* \(d=q\): symmetric to the previous case, again \(p=q\).

* \(d=5p\): then \(D=q\).  Since \(D<d\) this contradicts \(d<D\).

* \(d=5q\): similarly impossible.

Thus the only possibilities are  

* \(p=q\) (any prime), or  
* \(\{p,q\}=\{3,11\}\).

Hence  
\[
p=q\;\;\text{or}\;\;(p,q)=(3,11)\;\text{or}\;(11,3).
\]
